title: Mixed ASC/DESC ORDER BY Needs Matching Key Directions
description: An all-ascending index can't satisfy an ORDER BY that mixes ASC and DESC; the index key directions must match the sort. Why it matters: multi-column sorts with mixed directions (e.g. category ascending, price descending) show up constantly in product listings and reports -- and this is a subtle, common way indexing them goes wrong.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Most developers know the general rule that 'an index can supply an ORDER BY without a separate Sort step, if the index is already sorted in the order you want' — that's a pretty widely known optimization. What's much less widely known is a second, sharper requirement hiding inside that rule: it's not enough for the index to have the *right columns in the right order*. The *direction* each column is sorted in — ascending or descending — has to line up too, and getting this wrong is an extremely common and easy mistake precisely because it's so rarely mentioned.

Think about a phone book sorted by last name, and within each last name, by first name — that's a two-column sort, both ascending (A to Z). If someone asks 'give me everyone sorted by last name A-to-Z, and within each last name, first name Z-to-A' (i.e., mixed directions — one column ascending, the other descending), the existing phone book doesn't actually answer that. You could read it forward (getting last-name-ascending, first-name-ascending) or read the whole thing backward, back to front (getting last-name-descending, first-name-descending) — but there's no way to read a book that mixes 'forward for this column, backward for that one' just by choosing a direction to flip through the pages, because the physical order on the page only supports exactly one consistent direction throughout.

That is precisely the situation in this lesson: a query wants `ORDER BY Category ASC, Price DESC` — categories alphabetically, but within each category, the most expensive products first. There's already a composite index built as `(Category ASC, Price ASC)` — both columns ascending. Reading that index **forward**, from its first page to its last, delivers rows in `Category ASC, Price ASC` order — categories alphabetical, but prices cheapest-first within each category, the *opposite* of what's wanted. Reading the exact same index **backward**, from its last page to its first, delivers `Category DESC, Price DESC` — both columns flipped, which doesn't match either, because now the categories themselves are in the wrong direction. Neither forward nor backward gives you `Category ASC, Price DESC`. SQL Server's optimizer understands this limitation perfectly well — B-tree indexes (the underlying sorted-tree data structure behind a standard index) can only be walked in one of two ways, forward or backward, and both of those walks preserve or flip *every* column's direction together, never independently per column. Since neither available walk matches the requested mixed order, the optimizer has no choice but to fall back to reading the data (in whichever order it can get it) and then performing an explicit **Sort** operator afterward to rearrange it into the actually-requested order.

This is a genuinely sneaky trap because, at first glance, everything looks like it should just work: there IS a composite index on exactly the two columns the query sorts by, in exactly the right column order (Category first, then Price) — which is the part most people remember to check. It's easy to see 'index exists on (Category, Price), query sorts by Category then Price, so why is there still a Sort in the plan?' and be genuinely puzzled, because the piece that's actually wrong — the *direction* of the second column — is invisible unless you specifically go look at how the index was defined and compare it, column by column, against the ORDER BY's ASC/DESC markers.

Why does this situation come up constantly in real applications, rather than being some rare edge case? Because 'sort by category, but within each category rank by something descending — price, quality score, popularity, most-recent-first' is an extremely natural and common request in product listings, leaderboards, and reports: 'show categories alphabetically, but within each, the priciest item first' or 'show each region, and within it, the top salesperson first.' Any time a sort mixes an ascending grouping column with a descending 'rank within group' column, this exact index-direction mismatch is lying in wait, and most indexes get created with a default of all-ascending unless someone deliberately thinks about the direction the query actually needs.

The fix is precise and mechanical once you understand the underlying rule: build the index with matching directions per column — `(Category ASC, Price DESC)` in this case — so a single forward read of the index naturally produces categories alphabetically and, within each one, prices from highest to lowest, exactly matching the requested ORDER BY with no rearranging needed. The general principle to carry forward: for a multi-column sort, an index only eliminates the Sort operator if its column order matches AND every column's direction matches (or the entire set of directions is uniformly flipped, which also works since a full backward scan is always available) — column order alone is necessary but not sufficient.

## Scenario
A listing orders products by `Category` ascending, then `Price` **descending**. There's already a composite index on `(Category, Price)` — yet the plan still does a Sort. The index looks right, but its **direction** is wrong.

## Why it's slow
`IX_Products_Cat_Price_ASC` stores rows as `Category ASC, Price ASC`. The query wants `Category ASC, Price DESC`. Reading the index **forward** gives `Price ASC`; reading it **backward** gives `Category DESC, Price DESC` — neither matches `Category ASC, Price DESC`. A single index scan can't produce a *mixed* ordering, so SQL Server adds an explicit **Sort**.

## What to look for
- A Sort operator despite a composite index that covers the same columns.
- The `ORDER BY` mixes ASC and DESC across columns; the index is uniform ASC.

## The concept
To satisfy a **mixed-direction** `ORDER BY` without sorting, the index key directions must match it (or be the exact reverse of all of them). Build the index as `(Category ASC, Price DESC)`. Now an ordered forward scan yields exactly `Category ASC, Price DESC` and the Sort disappears. Column *order* isn't enough — for multi-column sorts, direction matters too.
hints: The existing index is (Category ASC, Price ASC), but you want Price DESC within each Category. Forward or backward, the index can't produce that mixed order.
For a mixed ASC/DESC sort, the index key directions must match the ORDER BY.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Products_Cat_PriceDesc ON Products(Category ASC, Price DESC); then re-run.
